doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Junior Mance's Harlem Lullaby and Monk Rowe's listening memory
summary: Monk Rowe says a Junior Mance record Dorn produced was his first Dorn connection. Dorn recalls putting a harpsichord on the blues tune.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well I was a Joel Dorn fan before I even knew who you were.
Thank you.
Okay, I have a little story. When I was about in junior high —
Is this another record I made?
Uh huh. I used to listen — do you remember the name Harry Abraham?
Yeah.
He was a jazz DJ in Rochester.
Right.
And he had a voice like yours.
We all had the same voice. You’re listening to jazz at 96 point five in Philadelphia. You know everybody was like a pretentious schmuck.
Yeah well, but late at night I used to take my little transistor radio to bed with me and listen to him at night.
I used to do that with the black AM stations so I could hear doo wop when I was in like ninth grade. So I know what you mean.
Well one night this song came on.
I hope I remember it.
[audio interlude]
Junior Mance. It’s “Darling Je Vous Aime Beaucoup,” but he calls it “Harlem Lullaby.” Yeah.
“Harlem Lullaby.” And I just thought this song had something, I just loved it. I didn’t know who Junior Mance was.
Yeah. Isn’t it pretty?
And so that was my first Joel Dorn like thing.
Really.
But it wasn’t until I started talking to you about the Joe Williams thing and I started getting out — and I said oh he produced my favorite record.
Isn’t that wild.
That was cool.
Yeah well Junior’s a great player.
Do you remember that session at all?

I remember that session because Junior was one of the guys I thought, you know, could be commercial in the sense of a Ramsey Lewis or an Oscar Peterson or an Ahmad Jamal, one of those guys. He never quite reached that level you know. I loved the way he played. So I think on that record my brilliant idea was to have him play a blues on a harpsichord?
Yes.
“What Becomes of the Broken Hearted” it became a Motown tune.
That was on the record.
You know, had I left Junior to his own devices generally I think he would have made better records. But some of the things that I suggested worked. Some didn’t.
Well I just wanted to play that.
I love that. That was his, and he really loved that song.
